newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.
newsitem.headline: AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.

text.p: Australian Meat and Livestock Corp's (AMLC) weekly export prices are as follows:

AMLC COMMENTARY: Australian saleyards were inundated with cattle and sheep this week, the first full working week after the Easter holiday period.

Queensland yardings rose by 7,500 head to 21,000 head, Victoria's rose by 6,000 head to 16,000 head and New South Wales (NSW) numbers rose 12,600 head to 31,500 head. Sheep and lamb numbers also rose significantly.
Many producers, especially in central and southern NSW, South Australia, Victoria and Tasmania, have been encouraged to clear decks by the onset of cooler weather and looming frosts.

Throughout these regions, pasture growth and surplus feed availability have been stilted by the poor seasonal conditions endured since the summer of 1996. Large offerings can be expected to continue until these areas receive an autumn break.

Tight pasture conditions are now encompassing many areas of NSW. Cattle yardings of 31,500 head at Livestock Market Reporting Service Centres were the highest on record, eclipsing the previous highest yardings of 28,700 head in October 1994.

Despite much larger yardings, livestock prices, although easier in most sales, held up reasonably well. In Queensland the extra numbers were matched by relatively vigorous processor buying, and slaughter activity also increased with the resumption of full working weeks. In other states, processor buying was less certain and more selective and generally only the best bullocks, cows and trade cattle held last week's rates.

Yearling cattle and vealers, however, were heavily discounted in NSW and Victoria. Price falls were related to both a general deterioration in quality and heavier numbers. In Victoria, the state yearling steer indicator fell by 5.6 cents a kg liveweight to 90.7 cents a kg and in NSW the price fall was four cents a kg to 87 cents a kg.

In export beef markets, U.S. imported manufacturing beef prices turned three to nine Australian cent a kg lower with increased supplies. Entries to the U.S. of imported frozen beef increased by about 40 percent over the past fortnight. The bulk of the increase was supplied by New Zealand packers and to a lesser extent Australian exporters. Supplies from New Zealand can be expected to remain high in the near term.
Prices for U.S. domestic product firmed on packer concerns of extreme Mid-west weather, with floods and blizzards.
In Japan the weakening yen overwhelmed other considerations such as buying for the Golden Week holiday and lower stock levels, keeping the market on the back foot.

Offer prices for Australian product remained steady on the last week despite the Japanese Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries confirmation that stock levels had fallen further in February.
A survey by the Japanese Management and Co-ordination Agency indicated that consumption of beef at home declined by 8.5 percent in February, disturbing news.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
